title: The subject, its countersubject, and the answer
caption: The first fugue opens with the subject in the viola under the dotted countersubject, which the first violin has been playing since the downbeat. S1 moves on beats 2 and 4, S2 on beats 1 and 3: two complete phrases, metrically out of phase, in invertible counterpoint. S2 is one line, not two: it leaps a compound interval on every offbeat, so on the page it reads as a pair of parallel strands. At m. 35 the cello answers in green — the same phrase a fifth lower, semitone for semitone, with no tonal adjustment.

title: Overtura, mm. 1–10: the subject in octaves
caption: No harmony, no counterpoint: the nine notes alone, each one held under a fermata, the whole quartet in octaves. The chromatic wedge is exposed before a bar of fugue is heard.

title: Overtura, mm. 26–30: the syncopated version
caption: First violin alone, pp, sempre pp. The subject now sits on the weak beats, written as tied eighths (Albrechtsberger’s Unterbrechung). This is the form in which the fugue will take it up.

title: First fugue, mm. 39–46: violin II, then violin I
caption: Violin II takes the subject an octave up, violin I the answer (with a chromatic C as a lead-in). Four entries, four bars apart, alternating between B flat and F: the exposition closes where it began.

title: Meno mosso e moderato, mm. 159–166
caption: The lyric stance: G flat major, pp, flowing sixteenths in the first violin against a descending line in the lower voices. Kerman hears "an almost blinding innocence" here. The same subject, now sung rather than argued.

title: Allegro molto e con brio, mm. 233–240
caption: The dance stance: 6/8, ff, gigue-like, the subject hammered out in the upper voices over a stamping bass. This is the scherzo of the piece — and the passage in which the motif is dismembered rather than affirmed.

title: Final fugue, mm. 273–280: the subject augmented
caption: The cello states the subject one note to the bar in A flat, while the upper voices answer with its diminished form. The learned style returns, and with it the subject’s pride of place.

title: First fugue, mm. 139–146: the subject at double speed
caption: Third variation: the viola takes the subject at double speed, the first violin the dotted countersubject in triplets, its leaps stretched beyond two octaves. The section does not resolve: it breaks off and slides to G flat.
